2026 SEMA Show • 2027 Toyota Crown Signia Gets GT-S Concept Treatment for SEMA, Becomes a Sleek Wagon
With the Model S/X and Cybertruck Gone and No New Models, Tesla Is Disappearing Before Our Very Eyes
25 photos
Photo: Tesla, edited
We've already known that Tesla is no longer interested in car manufacturing, even before the Model S and Model X were pronounced dead in January. The demise of the Cybertruck only confirms this strategy shift. However, the fact that Tesla has no new car model in the pipeline shows that we're looking at what airplane pilots call "controlled flight into terrain."
When Musk announced in January during the Q4 2025 earnings call that the Model S and Model X would be retired, I knew that was only the beginning. At the time, Musk's plan to merge his companies into one giant corporation under his control was already well known. The first step of this plan was completed in February, when SpaceX bailed money-losing xAI . However, Tesla was a different beast.
The company had a solid market position, with a sane business, which Musk no longer controlled after selling shares to buy Twitter. Tesla was too big a fish to swallow even for SpaceX, which only recently posted its first profitable quarter. At the time, I argued that Musk doesn't want a strong Tesla; he'd be better served if it went into the ground. That's how I look at all the steps Musk and Tesla have been taking in 2026. And sure enough, he seems to be doing a remarkable job at making Tesla worthless.
From sustainable mobility to amazing abundance In 2022, Tesla appeared to be on top of the world, with demand through the roof and prices that defied gravity. Sales were booming, and Musk thought selling 20 million cars per year by 2030 was a no-brainer. A year later, market conditions changed, and sales dropped. This apparently caused great distress, because Musk made some erratic business decisions.
First, he decided that the economy was crashing and started preparing Tesla for the impact. Budgets were cut, and employees were fired, sometimes indiscriminately. Those who refused to let enough people go, such as Supercharger chief Rebecca Tinucci, were fired themselves . Others, including Drew Baglino, Tesla's Senior VP of Powertrain and Energy, and Martin Viecha, VP of Investor Relations, left voluntarily.
Second, Musk decided that EVs were no longer cool enough, and doubled down on autonomous driving efforts. Tesla had already announced plans to develop a humanoid robot in 2022. By the time cars became uncool, the Tesla Optimus program showed some progress, and Musk thought that driverless cars and robots, or robots on wheels and robots on legs, were the new future.
Photo: Tesla The "not a carmaker" mantra originated in this bizarre strategic pivot. As vehicle sales started to disappoint, Musk and his minions declared that deliveries were irrelevant, because Tesla is now an artificial intelligence and robotics company, not a carmaker. The bad thing is that Musk started believing this himself, and the company started moving away from vehicle manufacturing. Even worse was that Tesla sucked at both robots and autonomous driving.
First, they came for the Model S and X; then, they came for the Cybertruck The Gen-3 compact EV was the first victim of this change. Despite Musk's denial, the affordable EV, known as Project Redwood, was scrapped the moment Musk announced that Tesla moved its production from Mexico to Texas , in December 2023. When media outlets reported that the compact EV was no more, Musk called them liars and announced the Cybercab demo event.
Musk knew very well that Tesla had abandoned work on the Gen 3 platform. However, he pretended that affordable models were still on the menu. And they were, but not as new cars based on the revolutionary Gen-3 platform, but as stripped-down variants of the existing Model 3 and Model Y. Sold at lower prices, these energized Tesla vehicle sales in 2026, especially as the world faced an oil crisis that sent fuel prices into the stratosphere.
However, as car buyers started prioritizing their budgets, the market for $80k vehicles crashed, affecting sales of all other Tesla models. The Model S, Model X, and the Cybertruck were already counted in the "Other Vehicles" category. Now, this category started shrinking by the quarter. Unsurprisingly, Tesla announced in January that the Model S and Model X would stop production in the second quarter of 2026.
Photo: Tesla At the time, I wondered how long it would take before the Cybertruck shared their fate. The Model S and Model X were developed a long time ago, and development costs were already covered, probably many times over. However, the Cybertruck was a technological showcase, which was very expensive to develop. Selling it in low numbers must've cost Tesla a lot of money.
Now, Elon Musk confirmed that the Cybertruck will go to play with the Model S and Model X on the playground of automotive history. The move was hardly unexpected after Tesla announced to reservation holders in Australia and New Zealand in October that the right-hand variant has been canceled.
What's coming up next? The Model S, Model X, and even the Cybertruck were prime candidates for removal, considering their lackluster sales. Nobody expected them to last very long, even though some hoped that Tesla would remake the Cybertruck into a full-size SUV, or at least a traditionally-looking pickup truck. Despite these expectations, killing the Cybertruck caused quite a stir in the Tesla community.
Not because the carmaker decided to cut its losses and canceled the money-losing models. Every company makes such decisions, however painful they might be. Still, the Cybertruck, despite its many failures, was considered a symbol of Tesla engineering prowess. Killing it means that Tesla also kills its most promising technologies, including its first 800-volt platform, the 48-volt low-voltage system, steer-by-wire, and more.
Photo: Tesla There's another reason to mourn, though. Killing a vehicle model is not tragic. Not having anything to replace it or to add to the lineup is actually worse. No new vehicle model is in Tesla's pipeline, if we don't count the Roadster. However, the flying car is not a new vehicle; it's a PR stunt. Even if it were produced, it would not change anything for Tesla.
The Cybertruck's demise, especially after the Model S and Model X were scrapped, confirms that Tesla doesn't want to make cars anymore. It might not want to sell products to consumers at all, not just vehicles. And that makes a lot of people uncomfortable. What would they upgrade their Tesla to? A Cybercab? That's a hard pass for anyone who is not blinded by Musk's nonsense.
Model 3, which sells slightly worse than the Model Y, will absolutely be next on the chopping block. And how long will the Model Y survive? It's still a very popular EV today, but, like the Model 3, is underpinned by a ten-year-old vehicle platform. It will soon start failing new crash safety standards, and Tesla might decide that developing a successor is not worth investing in.
Is Tesla still alive? And why should it? It's already clear that Tesla will be folded into SpaceX and disappear as an entity altogether. SpaceX is not interested in its car manufacturing business, or insurance, or charging. "Where we're going, we don't need roads." It might find value in driverless cars like the Cybercab and robots and the software that powers them, but the rest? The best we can hope is a spin-off so that somebody else continues Tesla legacy.
Photo: Alcides Antunes/Instagram Even though Musk and his fans argue that the Cybercab is the future , this will not be the car people expect, and will likely sell in far smaller numbers than Musk wants us to believe. He already announced that Tesla would not sell the Cybercab to consumers, but to businesses. Outside big cities, nobody would want to hail a cab for their day-to-day errands. People very much want to own their cars, and most of them, even to drive them.
I am certain that the Cybercab, robots, and autonomous driving are just a fad and will be replaced with other moonshot projects. Musk is very good at selling new dreams when the old ones lose their appeal. We already see this with the Terafab chip-making project. In five years, there will be something else.
One thing is almost certain, though: Musk doesn't want Tesla to be very valuable. He wants SpaceX to buy it at the lowest possible price, strip it of its most valuable assets, and eventually sell the rest piece by piece. Tesla has already started outsourcing Supercharger buildout, so the process has started. The time is of the essence, so a move is expected to be announced next month during the annual shareholder meeting .
